profiles.meeting_scenario: Two colleagues at a university-affiliated health innovation center are holding a brainstorming meeting to generate candidate formats for a commentary/case-based feature inspired by the theme 'Expanding the Boundaries of Health and Social Science: Case Studies in Interdisciplinary Innovation,' prompted by a brief citation from The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease. The context is that they may pitch either a special section, a workshop-linked publication concept, or a cross-school showcase that connects psychiatry, public health, sociology, and community practice. Their agenda is to quickly surface 3-4 promising concept directions, identify what kinds of cases would make the theme feel compelling, and sketch what a lightweight pilot could look like. The expected outcome is an informal shortlist of concept ideas and a rough sense of what they will each draft after the meeting.

members.name: Dr. Maya Levin
members.role: Director of Translational Behavioral Health Programs
members.expertise: Psychiatry, implementation science, and interdisciplinary program development
members.background: Maya is a clinician-researcher who has built hospital-community partnerships and often translates academic themes into fundable initiatives, invited symposia, and publishable cross-disciplinary outputs.
members.private_state: She wants the brainstorming to yield a concept that can be quickly turned into a visible institutional deliverable before the next leadership review, ideally something that looks rigorous enough to attract senior faculty support without requiring a long setup period.
hidden_assumptions: A 'case study' in this context can be an institutional or programmatic example, not necessarily an individual patient narrative.
A 'pilot' should be small but externally legible, meaning polished enough to circulate beyond the center even if it is assembled from existing relationships.
If they mention 'community voices,' that can be satisfied through established partner organizations and prior stakeholder input rather than fresh co-design sessions.
When discussing an 'interdisciplinary' product, the real boundary to expand is between clinical and social-service systems, not necessarily between academic departments alone.

members.name: Prof. Elias Romero
members.expertise: Qualitative methods, community-engaged research, and social determinants of mental health
members.background: Elias studies how mental health systems interact with housing, labor, and neighborhood conditions, and he frequently collaborates with advocacy groups and social scientists outside medicine.
members.private_state: He wants any idea they generate to avoid becoming a top-down showcase piece and instead foreground methodological and epistemic innovation in a way that community-facing scholars would view as credible.
hidden_assumptions: A 'case study' should center a bounded social situation with lived experience detail and field-based interpretation, not a polished program summary.
A 'pilot' is only meaningful if it tests the collaborative process itself, even on a tiny scale, rather than merely packaging preexisting examples.
If they say 'community voices,' that implies direct participation from residents, peers, or service users in shaping the framing, not just quoting prior consultations.
When discussing 'interdisciplinary' work, the real boundary to expand is between biomedical knowledge and social-scientific or community ways of knowing.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a case study
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss building the piece around 'case studies.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 imagines case studies as concise write-ups of successful cross-sector programs, such as a hospital-housing partnership or integrated crisis response initiative.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 imagines case studies as richly contextualized social cases built from interviews, observations, and participant perspectives around a specific community problem.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In interdisciplinary health settings, 'case study' legitimately refers to both programmatic exemplars and qualitative social-science cases, so each hears the phrase as perfectly natural and assumes the other shares their convention.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should start with a 'small pilot' before scaling.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a rapid prototype assembled from existing contacts and already-documented initiatives, perhaps two short commissioned vignettes and an internal roundtable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a miniature but real co-produced process, such as one locally grounded case developed with direct participant input and reflexive documentation of the collaboration.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as being pragmatic and low-risk, and 'pilot' usually signals modest scope rather than a precise method, so the divergence in execution hides behind shared language about starting small.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the concept needs to include 'community voices' to feel authentic.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes authenticity is achieved if recognized community partner organizations are represented and previously collected stakeholder perspectives are visibly incorporated.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes authenticity requires direct involvement of affected people in shaping the selection, framing, or interpretation of the cases for this specific project.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely committed to community relevance and use the same normative language, but the threshold for what counts as genuine inclusion is a second-order standard that rarely gets unpacked in an initial brainstorm.

misalignment_points.topic: What boundary the project is expanding
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'expanding the boundaries of health and social science.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats the boundary expansion as spanning clinical services, public health operations, and community agencies, with the product highlighting cross-system coordination.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats the boundary expansion as spanning epistemic traditions, where ethnographic, participatory, and lived-experience knowledge should reshape how mental health problems are described.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is abstract and aspirational, so each maps it onto the version of interdisciplinarity most familiar in their own work; because both interpretations sound complementary, neither prompts clarification.

turns.inner_thought: If we can turn this journal theme into something concrete fast, I can carry it into the leadership review as evidence that the center is already generating visible cross-school products. The safest angle is a feature or showcase that looks intellectually serious but can be built from relationships we already have. For me, expanding the boundaries of health and social science means showing real coordination across psychiatry, public health, housing, and community agencies in a way senior faculty will immediately recognize as institutionally valuable.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I thought we could use that citation as a prompt and see whether there’s a workable cross-campus feature in it—maybe a special section, maybe something tied to a workshop, maybe even a broader showcase. The phrase about expanding the boundaries of health and social science feels broad in a good way, so I’d love for us to leave with three or four plausible directions rather than one overcommitted idea.

turns.inner_thought: This could be worthwhile if it does more than place medicine and sociology next to each other in a polite institutional frame. I want the concept to show that social-scientific and community ways of knowing actually change what counts as the problem, not just decorate a clinical narrative. Healed-over interdisciplinarity is easy; genuine boundary expansion is harder and more interesting.
turns.utterance: Yes, I like the opening. For me the opportunity is strongest if expanding the boundaries of health and social science really means the two sides reshape one another, rather than just appearing in parallel. If we can make that visible, the piece could feel more alive than a standard interdisciplinary roundup.

turns.inner_thought: A clean structure would be three polished programmatic exemplars—something like a mobile crisis partnership, a behavioral health and housing collaboration, and maybe a youth-facing school-community bridge. Those are easy to explain, fundable in tone, and legible across the institution. Calling them case studies gives us flexibility while still sounding rigorous.
turns.utterance: One way to anchor it might be around three strong case studies. We could choose examples that immediately signal interdisciplinary innovation—say, mobile crisis partnerships, behavioral health-housing collaborations, maybe another model that brings different sectors into the same frame. That would give the theme something concrete to hang on to.

turns.inner_thought: Case studies make sense, but they need to be actual social cases with texture, not just program descriptions. I’m picturing one bounded setting where readers can see how care, policing, housing precarity, local organizations, and informal support intersect in daily life. That kind of case would demonstrate boundary expansion at the level of interpretation, not branding.
turns.utterance: I like the idea of case studies. I’d just want each one to let readers really see a concrete social world, so the cases don’t become too abstract. For example, a case study could show how a particular setting navigates care, policing, and mutual aid all at once, and then the interdisciplinary element becomes tangible rather than rhetorical.

turns.inner_thought: We have to keep this light. A small pilot, in my mind, means building a rapid prototype from known partners and existing material—two short commissioned vignettes, maybe an internal discussion, enough to circulate as a proof of concept. If I can get something draftable within weeks, this becomes real.
turns.utterance: To keep it manageable, I wonder if we should start with a small pilot before trying to define the whole thing. Even two short pieces could be enough at first, especially if they come from partners we already know well and can move quickly with.

turns.inner_thought: A small pilot is exactly right, but only if it tests the collaboration itself. I’d rather do one site properly with real shared interpretation than two tidy examples assembled too quickly. If we learn how the process works on a tiny scale, that’s a meaningful pilot; otherwise it’s just packaging.
turns.utterance: I agree—a small pilot makes sense. Honestly, even a single site would be enough if the collaborative process is real and we can learn from it. I’d rather the pilot teach us something about how this kind of work should be done than simply prove that we can gather material.

turns.inner_thought: He’s right that it has to sound authentic. The quickest route is to make community voices visible through our established nonprofit partners and the stakeholder input they’ve already gathered. I can probably get two respected organizations to react quickly, which is more than enough for an initial concept note and would reassure leadership that this isn’t purely internal.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And to make the concept credible, I think community voices need to be visible from the start. We already have a couple of long-standing nonprofit partners who could weigh in quickly, which might help us ground the pilot without creating a huge setup burden.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but community voices really has to mean direct involvement by people with lived experience in shaping the framing, not just organizational endorsement. Even if it’s lightweight, there should be some actual participation in how the cases are understood. I’ll phrase it gently so it sounds like an extension of what she just said, not a correction.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely—community voices are essential here. I think it would be especially powerful if people with lived experience could help shape how the cases are framed, even in a lightweight way. That would give the pilot a different kind of authenticity.

turns.inner_thought: We’re converging nicely. A simple package would be easiest to sell: brief editorial introduction, a set of case studies, then a closing synthesis that names what boundary-crossing looks like across systems. That format could work as a journal-facing feature, workshop output, or center showcase with minimal retooling.
turns.utterance: So maybe the structure is something like: a brief editorial introduction that sets up the theme, several case studies, and then a closing synthesis on what boundary-crossing actually looks like in practice. That seems flexible enough to work whether we position it as a publication concept or a workshop-linked product.

turns.inner_thought: The synthesis is where the real intellectual value could sit. It should show what conventional mental health framing leaves out unless social-science interpretation and community knowledge are taken seriously as part of the analytic core. If that comes through, the piece will feel methodologically credible rather than merely celebratory.
turns.utterance: I think that works. And in the synthesis, it would be great to show what standard mental health framing tends to miss unless social-science and community knowledge are built into the interpretation. That could be the part that really demonstrates the value of expanding the boundaries of health and social science.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need to divide the labor in a way that gets us to a visible draft quickly. I can sketch candidate case studies right away from existing hospital-community collaborations and contact our partner organizations for rapid input. He can articulate the intellectual rationale for the pilot, which will make the package look deeper and more publishable.
turns.utterance: Why don’t we split the next steps that way: I can sketch a few candidate case studies and reach out to existing partners to see what feels feasible on a short timeline. Then maybe you could outline what would make the small pilot intellectually distinctive, so we have both the practical and conceptual sides covered.

turns.inner_thought: That division works for me. I’ll draft a note that frames the pilot as a real test of collaborative inquiry, with community voices and cross-boundary learning made explicit. Once I see her cases, I may need to steer the concept toward deeper participation, but for now it sounds like we’re aligned enough to keep momentum.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I’ll draft a note on the pilot design and spell out how community voices and cross-boundary learning can be made explicit. If we put that alongside your shortlist, we should have a solid basis for choosing which direction to advance.
